E- and chemoselective thia-Michael addition to benzyl allenoate
Rifhat Bibi a, Amna Murtaza a, Khalid Mohammed Khan b, Zia ur Rehman a, Aamer Saeed a, Muhammad Nawaz
Tahirc, and Abbas Hassan a
aDepartment of Chemistry, Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad, Pakistan; bHEJ Research Institute of Chemistry, International Center for
Chemical and Biological Sciences, University of Karachi, Karachi, Pakistan; cDepartment of Physics, Sargodha University, Sargodha, Pakistan
ABSTRACT
Different thiols were successfully reacted with benzyl allenoate resulting in E-selective thia-Michael
addition product with a,b-unsaturation as confirmed by single crystal x-ray crystallographic ana-
lysis. The thia-Michael addition is chemoselective and free amine and alcohol groups were well
tolerated. Catalytic triethylamine was required for high conversion. Fair to excellent yields were
obtained for a variety of aliphatic, aryl and heteroaryl thiols.
GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT
ARTICLE HISTORY
Received 31 January 2020
Accepted 18 July 2020
KEYWORDS
Thia-Michael addition;
a-b-unsaturation;
E-selective; b-substituted
thioenoates; chemoselective
1. Introduction
Michael addition reaction is a widely utilized and historically
important reaction in organic synthesis. [1] It is more than a
century old reaction in which addition of soft nucleophiles to
electron deficient alkenes occurs. [2] The nucleophiles consist
of stabilized enolates, organocuprates, and oxygen, nitrogen
and sulfur anion or pronucleophiles. The electrophiles include
unsaturation attached to electron withdrawing groups such as
enone, enoate, enal, nitroalkene, alkene nitrile and analogous
alkyne compounds. Sulfur containing compounds are consid-
ered to be soft nucleophiles and the thia-Michael addition
reactions are well documented.
[3] a,b-Unsaturated carbonyl
compounds demonstrated their higher ability as Michael
acceptor when reacted with thiols.
[4] Similar reactivity
have been utilized to a great extent for the annulation and the
synthesis of diverse heterocyclic structures. [5]
Mostly the reaction reported for thia-Michael addition to
allenoate and alkynoates result the Z-isomer as main product.[6]
For instance, the thia-Michael addition to ethyl 2-methylbuta-
2,3-dienoate have been reported to give mixture of products in
the absence of any additive, favoring the conjugated Z-selective
Michael addition product.
[7] This is, however, not the case
when PBu3 was utilized as the catalyst and only the non-conju-
gated Michael addition product is observed (Scheme 1,r e a c t i o n
1). Recently, a nonselective thia-Michael addition of thiophenol
to methyl 2-butynoate in the presence of sodium hydroxide
has been reported to give 1:1 mixture of E/Z isomers.[6c]
Interestingly, the resulted b-substituted thioenoates upon fur-
ther reaction with in situ generated alkyl cuprates, afforded the
thiol-substituted products in stereospecific fashion (Scheme 1,
reaction 2). This methodology has been applied in the total syn-
thesis of juvenile hormones.
[6a]
Owing to the importance of the olefin selectivity in thia-
Michael addition, herein, we report a general and mild E-
selective and chemo-selective thia-Michael addition to benzyl
allenoate as surrogate for alkynoate.
2. Results and discussion
In a typical reaction, when thiophenol 1a was treated with
benzyl allenoate in THF with 150 mol% of triethylamine, it
resulted in benzyl b-phenylthio-2-butenoate 2a in 60% yield
as single E-isomer selectively. Lowering the amount of trie-
thylamine increased the yield and in the presence of only
20 mol% of triethylamine, 72% of 2a was isolated ( Table 1 ,
entries 1 and 2).
The catalytic amount of triethylamine was found to be
optimal for other examples as well. When 2-aminothiophe-
nol 1b was treated with benzyl allenoate and 20 mol% of
triethylamine, ( E)-benzyl 3-(2-aminophenylthio)but-2-enoate
2b was isolated in 68% yield. As the substrate contains an
ortho amino group, it was assumed that the reaction will not
require any additional triethylamine. Surprisingly, with only

10 mol% of triethylamine, 2b was isolated in 60% yield
while, in the absence of triethylamine only 26% of 2b was
isolated ( Table 1 , entries 4 and 5). This suggested that a
catalytic amount of triethylamine acts as proton shuttle. [8]
However, in the presence of 150 mol% of triethylamine, 2b
was isolated in much higher 92% yield as single E-isomer.
In the case of 2b, it was important to confirm the che-
moselectivity for thia vs aza-Michael addition and the
configuration of the double bond. Although NMR analysis
was useful, single crystal X-ray analysis confirmed the
structure of 2b. The product was indeed thia-Michael
adduct with E-enone geometry ( Figure 1 ). We were
unable to detect any Z-2b from the NMR analysis of the
crude reaction mixture. Interestingly, when the reaction
was carried out in the absence of triethylamine, ( Table 1 ,
entry 5), there was low conversion and in addition to the
product 2b, the reaction tube had minor amount of
physically different crystals than the crystals for 2b.I ts i n -
gle crystal X ray analysis showed unconjugated product
3b (Figure 1 ). All attempts to isolate the compound 3b in
large quantity and its spectroscopic characterization were
unsuccessful.
To check the scope of the reaction, a variety of thiols were
tested. Apart from 1a and 1b, when 2-amino-4-chlorobenze-
nethiol 1c was reacted with benzyl allenoate, thia-Michael
adduct 2c was formed in 93% yield. Again, no aza-Michael
adduct, or Z isomer was detected from reaction mixture.
Further aryl thiols including 2-bromobenzenethiol 1d and 2,6-
dichlorothiophenol 1e and 2-naphthalenethiol 1f under the
same reaction conditions resulted in Michael adducts 2d, 2e

and 2f in 84%, 82% and 68% yields, respectively. Furthermore,
heteroaryl thiols smoothly undergo thia-Michael addition to
benzyl allenoate. Benzo[d]thiazole-2-thiol 1g resulted in 83%
of the thia-Michael adduct 2g. 2-Pyridinethiol resulted in
quantitative yield of the desire product 2h. Similarly,
highly functionalized 5-(4-nitrophenyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazole-2-
thiol 1i effectively reacts in thia-Michael fashion under the
same reaction conditions to give 2i in 75% yield.
Aliphatic thiols were also exposed to thia-Michael add-
ition. 2-Mercaptoethanol afforded thia-Michael adduct 2j in
92% yield. In case of 2j thia-Michael adducts formation also
demonstrated that free hydroxyl does not play a competitive
role. Sterically demanding 2-methylpropane-2-thiol leads to
product 2k in 68% yield. A long chain aliphatic thiol dodec-
ane-1-thiol efficiently resulted in adduct 2l in 82% yield
(Scheme 2 ). The reaction scope suggested that the reaction
is general toward a variety of aliphatic, aryl, heteroaryl thiols
in the presence of free hydroxyl and amine functionality.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we were able to obtain E-selective thia-Michael
addition of aryl, heteroaryl and aliphatic thiols to benzyl
allenoate. The reaction is facilitated by catalytic amount of
triethylamine and is chemoselective toward thia-Michael
addition in the presence of free amine and alcohol func-
tional groups. The chemoselectivity and geometrical charac-
terization were confirmed though single crystal X-ray
analysis of 2b. Additional characterization details for the X-
ray structural studies are presented in the Supplemental
Materials ( Tables S1 and S2).
4. Experimental
Commercially available reagents were used without further
purification unless necessary. Solvents were dried and dis-
tilled before their use. Reactions to be run in non-aqueous
solvents were accomplished under an inert atmosphere of
nitrogen. For Michael addition reaction of thiol,
13 /C2 100 mm sealed test tubes were used. To dry combined
organic extracts, anhydrous sodium sulfate was used. Thin
Layer Chromatography (TLC) was used for monitoring the
reaction progress. UV visible spots were inspected under
UV light at 254 nm. For visualization of UV inactive spots,
different staining reagents such as potassium permanganate,
phosphomolybdic acid (PMA), anisaldehyde or ninhydrin
solution were used as appropriate. Flash column chromatog-
raphy using silica gel was performed for purification of most
of the products. Mass spectrometric (HRMS) experiments
were carried out on Finnigan MAT-311A (Germany) mass
spectrometer with (CI) ionization techniques. NMR spectra
were obtained using a Bruker 300 NMR MHz spectrometer
in deuterated solvents using TMS as internal reference, at
300 MHz (
1H NMR) and 75 MHz ( 13C NMR). Chemical
shifts are mentioned in delta ( d) units while coupling con-
stants ( J) values are in Hertz unit (Hz). The single crystal X-
rays analysis was carried out with a Bruker Kapa APEX-II
CCD diffractometer having a CCD detector set 40 mm from
the crystal. From a sealed ceramic diffraction tube
(SIEMENS) having graphite-monochromated Mo-K a radi-
ation, different intensities were determined. Then using
Patterson and DIRDIF method, the structure of the com-
pound was solved. The Supplemental Materials contains
sample
1H and 13C NMR spectra for the products 2 (Figures
S1 – S 25).
4.1. Synthesis of substrate benzyl buta-2,3-dienoate
The benzyl buta-2,3-dienoate was synthesize in a slightly
modified procedure to the previously reported method. [9]
See the Supplemental Materials for the detailed experimen-
tal procedure.
4.2. General procedure for the addition of different
thiols to allenoate
Oven-dried sealed tube was charged with benzyl buta-2,3-
dienoate (123 lL, 0.75 mmol, 150 mol%), distilled triethyl-
amine (19.2 lL, 0.1 mmol, 20 mol%) and nucleophile 1a-s
(0.5 mmol, 100 mol%). Freshly distilled THF (1 mL, 0.5 M) was
added and purged with nitrogen. The mixture was placed in
an oil bath at 70 /C14 C and was allowed to stir for 24 h. Solvent
was evaporated over dry silica gel and purification by flash col-
umn chromatography gave the desired product 2a-s.
